extracted.intended_audience: writers, artists, critics, and students of aesthetics/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply aesthetic principles for producing or judging works that aim at the sublime or the beautiful (how novelty, pain/pleasure, sympathy, taste, and decorum operate in affecting readers/viewers). Useful for critics and creative-writers shaping emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste is composite (sensibility, imagination, reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: “What is called taste, in its most general acceptation, is not a simple idea, but is partly made up of a perception of the primary pleasures of sense, of the secondary pleasures of the imagination, and of the conclusions of the reasoning faculty, concerning the various relations of these, and concerning the human passions, manners, and actions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'taste' as a compound faculty: sensory pleasure, imaginative pleasure, and rational judgment all contribute. The groundwork (senses) is common to all, so criticism can be reasoned about; do not treat taste as a single instinctual faculty. When evaluating or composing, consider how a work appeals across these three registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility vs. judgment — defects produce different failures of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: “So long as we are conversant with the sensible qualities of things, hardly any more than the imagination seems concerned... From a defect in the former of these qualities arises a want of taste; a weakness in the latter constitutes a wrong or a bad one.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose failures: blunt sensibility yields indifference (cannot be moved by subtle effects); weak judgment yields erroneous taste (misapplies principles, violates decorum). Remedies differ: increased sensibility through exposure and refinement; improved judgment through study, attention, and disciplined exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners, decorum, and observance of time/place are core to refined taste
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whatever certainty is to be acquired in morality and the science of life; just the same degree of certainty have we in what relates to them in works of imitation... our skill in manners, and in the observances of time and place, and of decency in general, ... is what is called taste.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A refined work must respect the conventions of manners, time, place, and decency appropriate to its genre and subject. Judgment in these matters is learned (Horace's schools): evaluate whether a work observes congruity and appropriateness before praising its imaginative or sensual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick/first impressions are not proof of true taste
rubrics_metrics.description: “One of this character can never be a refined judge... The excellence and force of a composition must always be imperfectly estimated from its effect on the minds of any, except we know the temper and character of those minds.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate immediate strong feeling with refined critical appreciation. Quick sensibility can produce strong but uncritical pleasure; reliable judgment often comes from cultivated experience and reflection. For creators: rely on considered structure and decorum, not only on immediate sensational hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty is necessary but insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first and the simplest emotion which we discover in the human mind is curiosity... Some degree of novelty must be one of the materials in every instrument which works upon the mind; and curiosity blends itself more or less with all our passions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use novelty to engage attention — but novelty alone cannot sustain long-term effect. Combine novelty with deeper powers (pain/pleasure, sympathy, moral relations) for durable emotional impact. Avoid novelty for its own sake (giddiness, restlessness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish positive pleasure from 'delight' (pleasure from removal of pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burke introduces the term 'delight' to express the sensation which accompanies the removal of pain or danger, distinguishing it from 'pleasure' which is positive and independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting emotional arcs, recognize different felt qualities: positive pleasures (musical beauty, sweetness) feel different from the relief or awe that follows danger's removal. Use this distinction to modulate reader response (e.g., relief after peril should not be written as the same as sensual pleasure).

rubrics_metrics.name: The difference between removal-of-pain and positive pleasure matters for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: “We shall venture to propose, that pain and pleasure are not only not necessarily dependent... but that, in reality, the diminution or ceasing of pleasure does not operate like positive pain; and that the removal or diminution of pain, in its effect, has very little resemblance to positive pleasure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how audiences experience relief, disappointment, indifference, or grief differently than direct pleasures or pains. Avoid conflating these in description or emotional pacing — e.g., the relief after danger is sober and awe‑tinged, not smoothly voluptuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the dynamics of cessation: indifference, disappointment, grief
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cessation of pleasure affects the mind three ways. If it simply ceases after having continued a proper time, the effect is indifference; if it be abruptly broken off, there ensues an uneasy sense called disappointment; if the object be so totally lost that there is no chance of enjoying it again, a passion arises... called grief.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narrative or lyrical losses with attention to whether the loss is temporary, abrupt, or permanent — each produces distinct emotional states and aesthetic effects (indifference, disappointment, grieving). Leverage these to shape tonal transitions and character responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime = what excites ideas of pain, danger, or terror
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whatever is fitted in any sort to excite the ideas of pain and danger... or operates in a manner analogous to terror, is a source of the sublime; that is, it is productive of the strongest emotion which the mind is capable of feeling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To aim for the sublime, foreground elements that suggest pain, danger, vastness, or terror. Recognize that the sublime relies on the power of those ideas (pain, death) — deploy them with care and modulation rather than gratuitous shock. Consider scale, threat, and existential stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance and modification make terror delightful
rubrics_metrics.description: “When danger or pain press too nearly, they are incapable of giving any delight, and are simply terrible; but at certain distances, and with certain modifications, they may be, and they are, delightful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position threatening elements so they are perceived at a psychological or aesthetic distance (fictional framing, representation, safe remove) to permit pleasurable engagement with terror. Use mediation (symbol, artifice, narrative distance) to make fearful imagery enjoyable rather than overwhelming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is a social quality that produces attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: “I call beauty a social quality; for ... when men and women ... give us a sense of joy and pleasure in beholding them ... they inspire us with sentiments of tenderness and affection... we like to have them near us, and we enter willingly into a kind of relation with them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray beauty not just as sensory patterning but as a social magnet: beauty in characters or objects should plausibly invite attachment and relational interest. Use beauty to justify desire, affiliation, and social bonds in narrative or description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions cluster around self-preservation and society — use accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: “Most of the ideas which are capable of making a powerful impression on the mind... may be reduced very nearly to these two heads, self-preservation, and society; to the ends of one or the other of which all our passions are calculated to answer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify emotional strategies: appeals to self-preservation (danger, pain) are apt to produce the sublime; appeals to society (generation, friendship) are apt to produce beauty and social pleasures. Tailor plot, stakes, and imagery to the dominant cluster you want to activate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy (identification) is the mechanism by which arts transfuse passions
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is by the first of these passions (sympathy) that we enter into the concerns of others; that we are moved as they are moved... It is by this principle chiefly that poetry, painting, and other affecting arts, transfuse their passions from one breast to another, and are often capable of grafting a delight on wretchedness, misery, and death itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empathetic detail, psychological realism, and vantage-point techniques to elicit sympathy; sympathy lets audiences take pleasure in represented misfortune (tragedy). Do not over-attribute the effect to explicit reasoning — sympathy is often automatic and bodily; craft sensory and situational triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the sufferer excellent to heighten aesthetic delight in misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our delight, in cases of this kind, is very greatly heightened, if the sufferer be some excellent person who sinks under an unworthy fortune.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To intensify tragic or sublime pleasure, center the distress on morally or socially admirable figures: noble victims amplify the audience's sympathetic engagement and heighten the aesthetic effect of their fall or suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitude versus society: absolute solitude is extreme pain; partial solitude can be agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Absolute and entire solitude, that is, the total and perpetual exclusion from all society, is as great a positive pain as can almost be conceived... Good company, lively conversations, and the endearments of friendship, fill the mind with great pleasure; a temporary solitude, on the other hand, is itself agreeable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts between solitude and society to produce emotional texture. Total, permanent isolation should be portrayed as extreme negative affect; temporary solitude can be restorative. This informs character arcs and tonal balances between action and contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate taste by extending knowledge, steady attention, and frequent exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am convinced that the understanding operates... and nothing else; and its operation is in reality far from being always sudden... the taste ... is improved exactly as we improve our judgment, by extending our knowledge, by a steady attention to our object, and by frequent exercise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For creators and critics: deliberate practice, study of exemplars, and sustained attentive reading/seeing build reliable taste and judgment. Encourage methods (reading classics, studying manners/genres) rather than relying on instant aesthetic intuition.
